title: Calibrating Africa’s green industrialization strategy, Part 2
body:
Africa remains largely on the periphery of the global green economy. Yet a few countries—most notably South Africa, Morocco, and Tunisia—are beginning to emerge as the continent’s green innovation and manufacturing hubs, as illustrated in the figure. While encouraging, this early momentum remains fragmented, uncoordinated, and insufficient to shift Africa’s overall position in global green economy.

- The reality is stark: no single African country possesses the full set of technological, financial, infrastructural, and institutional capabilities required to compete globally in complex green technology value chains. African nations are archetypes of what economists call late industrializers, and their historical challenges in pursuing industrialization are well documented. Layered onto these are the geopolitical complexities of green industrialization, which further heighten the hurdles.

Yet there is a viable path forward: regionalized industrial strategy. By coordinating across borders, African countries can collectively create green manufacturing ecosystems that initially serve local and regional markets, while building capabilities that, over the medium to long term, enable African firms to compete meaningfully in global green technology value chains.

The critical question, then, is: how can Africa integrate its scattered opportunities—its green minerals, untapped energy potential, skills, and nascent green innovation hubs—into a cohesive, continentwide strategy that elevates its role from periphery to gatekeeper in the global green economy?

Consider the possibilities: cobalt mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo could be processed in Zambia, components manufactured in South Africa could be assembled into batteries or EVs in Morocco, creating an interconnected, continentwide value chain. Such integration would transform Africa’s scattered assets into a strategic, competitive green industrial ecosystem.

- The strategy is clear: regionalization is the way forward. However, Africa must move decisively to the next stage—designing and implementing regional green technology production networks that are functional, coordinated, and capable of positioning the continent as an active and competitive player in the global green economy.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD
